issues: The significance overstates the source. It says the census 'extract[ed] exactly the data that fed persecution', which implies the cards were used to find Jews for deportation. The cited Bundesarchiv essay says the opposite. Their use for the deportations 'could not be proved so far ... and is rather unlikely', because the cards reached the registration offices only in April/May 1941 and the Reich Office of Genealogy only from January 1942. The USHMM source also stresses that census data served in aggregate and that identifying victims 'did not rely on modern technology'. The significance is rewritten so it keeps what is documented (a broken 'purely statistical' promise; identifying racial data sent to a Nazi genealogy office) without claiming the cards drove deportations.

Summary: 'the surviving cards name about 277,500 people' is imprecise. The essay counts about 277,500 people of Jewish origin under the Nazi classification, in about 130,000 households. The cards covered everyone in a household, so they also record many non-Jewish people (Table 1: 410,920 people in total on the cards passed on). Reworded.

Checked OK: census date 17 May 1939; the 16 June 1933 census asked about religion; a supplementary card for each household; 'massive penalties' threatened; sealed envelope; 'purely statistical evaluation'; cards with a Jewish grandparent passed to the Reich Office of Genealogy after statistical processing. Central-Berlin coordinates are fine (flagged in locationNote).

fieldFixes.summary: Germany's census of 17 May 1939 came with a supplementary card for each household asking whether any grandparent was Jewish, where the 16 June 1933 census had asked about religion. Respondents were threatened with heavy penalties for false answers but promised discretion (cards in a sealed envelope) and “a purely statistical evaluation”. Cards recording a Jewish grandparent were nonetheless passed, after statistical processing, to the Reich Office of Genealogy. The surviving cards list about 277,500 people classed as of Jewish origin, in about 130,000 households, with names, birth dates and exact addresses. The Federal Archives says it has not been proved that the cards were used to prepare the deportations, and thinks it unlikely: they reached the registration offices only in April/May 1941 and the Genealogy Office in January 1942.
fieldFixes.significance: A census confidentiality promise was broken. “Racial” data collected for “a purely statistical evaluation” ended up, by name and address, in a Nazi genealogy office. Once data is collected, a promise to keep statistical and identifying data apart is only as strong as the regime holding it.

issues: The summary states as fact that 'Jewish refugees who had avoided registration died at a lower rate'. Seltzer and Anderson say that Jewish refugees from Germany and other countries living in the Netherlands had a lower death rate than Dutch Jews. They offer as the 'best explanation' that the refugees, 'unlike most Dutch Jews, avoided registration'. That is their interpretation, not an established fact, so the summary now attributes it.
Minor: source[0] is labelled accessType PAYWALL while the URL given is a freely readable course copy. The JSTOR original is paywalled. Left as is and flagged for the editor.

Checked OK: Methorst (director-general of the Dutch CBS, formerly head of population registration) reported in 1938 on the 'cradle to grave' system. Lentz is his successor as head of the registration office. By early 1941 there were special registers of Jews and 'Gypsies'. The identity cards played 'an important role'. The death rate was 73 percent. Page numbers 487-488 match the running heads. An independent check (nl.wikipedia, Jacobus Lambertus Lentz) confirms that Lentz headed the Rijksinspectie van de Bevolkingsregisters (The Hague), set up under the 1936 decree requiring a personal card for every inhabitant from 1 July 1936, and 'speelde ook een hoofdrol in de uitvoering van de aanmeldplicht voor Joden'.

fieldFixes.summary: Before the German occupation the Netherlands had completed a comprehensive population registration system, praised by statistics chief H. W. Methorst in 1938 for following each person “from cradle to grave”. By early 1941 his successor as head of the registration office, J. L. Lentz, had adapted it into special registers of Jews and Roma (“Gypsies”). These registers and the related identity cards played an important role in rounding them up before deportation. Dutch Jews had the highest death rate (73 percent) of Jews in any occupied western European country. Jewish refugees living in the Netherlands died at a lower rate. Demographers William Seltzer and Margo Anderson think the best explanation is that, unlike most Dutch Jews, the refugees avoided registration.

issues: Wrong states. The summary says the Census Bureau 'provided block-level data locating Japanese Americans in California and six other states'. This repeats a Scientific American sentence that lists California, Arizona, Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, Idaho and Arkansas. Those are the seven states that held the War Relocation Authority camps, and SciAm's own earlier sentence uses them for 'internment camps in California and six other states'. They are not where Japanese Americans lived before removal. Washington and Oregon, which had large pre-war communities, are missing from the list. Seltzer and Anderson's own peer-reviewed account (Social Research 2001, p. 492) says the Bureau helped 'the military authorities on the West Coast', with tract-level tabulations in January 1942 and census-block maps of Japanese Americans per block.

Misleading sequence. The summary puts the block-level help after the Second War Powers Act (March 1942), implying the Act enabled it. The tract tabulations date from January 1942, before the Act. Seltzer and Anderson also note that before the Act was even introduced, the Census director said he was willing to ignore the law to let defense authorities check individual census records.
Typo: 'an 4 August 1943' should be 'a 4 August 1943'.

Checked OK: the Morgenthau request of 4 August 1943 for names and locations of people of Japanese ancestry in the Washington, D.C. area; released seven days later; found in Commerce Department chief clerk records by Anderson and Seltzer (PAA paper, 29-31 March 2007); confidentiality restored in 1947; the Act's wording 'in connection with the conduct of the war' (Ruggles & Magnuson, PDR 49(3), 2023, pp. 651-679, confirmed via PubMed metadata).

fieldFixes.summary: From January 1942 the Census Bureau helped the Army on the West Coast remove Japanese Americans. It supplied tract-level tabulations and census-block maps showing how many Japanese Americans lived on each block. The Second War Powers Act (March 1942) then let the Secretary of Commerce supply census information for the conduct of the war, suspending census confidentiality. In 2007 historian Margo Anderson and statistician William Seltzer showed from Commerce Department records that the Bureau had complied, within seven days, with a 4 August 1943 request from Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau. He had asked for the names and locations of all people of Japanese ancestry in the Washington, D.C., area. Congress restored census confidentiality in 1947.

fieldFixes.summary: On 8 February 1950 the GDR's Volkskammer passed, in a rushed procedure, a law turning the Interior Ministry's Main Administration for the Protection of the Economy into the Ministry for State Security. It took effect when President Wilhelm Pieck promulgated it on 18 February. In 1989 the ministry had 91,015 full-time employees (as of 31 October) and about 189,000 unofficial informers, one for every 89 citizens. Its surviving records run to more than 111 kilometres of files.

fieldFixes.summary: In “Privacy”, California Law Review vol. 48 no. 3 (August 1960), p. 383, Dean William L. Prosser of the University of California School of Law surveyed the case law since Warren and Brandeis. He concluded it was “not one tort, but a complex of four”: intrusion upon seclusion, public disclosure of embarrassing private facts, false-light publicity, and appropriation of name or likeness. Law professor Amy Gajda credits the article with substantially boosting the influence of Warren and Brandeis's essay, which courts cited far more often after 1960 than before.

fieldFixes.title: Vance Packard's The Naked Society sounds the alarm on surveillance
fieldFixes.summary: Journalist Vance Packard, author of The Hidden Persuaders, published The Naked Society (New York: David McKay, 1964), a popular exposé whose first part is titled “The Mounting Surveillance”. It opens by looking in on “a reasonably successful family in a typical city of the Land of Liberty, 1964”, who are watched at every turn. The mother is recorded by a closed-circuit TV camera hidden behind a mesh screen in a store dressing room. On 26 July 1966 Packard was the first witness when a House subcommittee on invasion of privacy opened hearings on proposals for a National Data Center.
fieldFixes.significance: It helped carry privacy out of the law reviews to a general readership worried about files, bugs and hidden cameras. Two years later lawmakers weighing a federal data bank called its author as their first witness.

issues: The significance says Griswold anchored constitutional privacy 'in personal autonomy rather than in property or place'. Douglas's majority opinion does not support that. It rests the right on the marital relationship and on place-based guarantees: the Third Amendment's 'in any house', the Fourth Amendment's 'persons, houses, papers, and effects', and 'Would we allow the police to search the sacred precincts of marital bedrooms ...?'. The autonomy reading came in later cases. Reworded to what the opinion says.

Checked OK: decided 7 June 1965, argued 29-30 March 1965 (U.S. Reports syllabus). Griswold was Executive Director of the Planned Parenthood League of Connecticut, and Buxton 'Medical Director for the League at its Center in New Haven'. They were convicted as accessories and fined $100 each for giving married persons information and medical advice on contraception, under a statute forbidding contraceptive use. Douglas wrote for the Court. Both quotes are verbatim. Coordinates are the Supreme Court Building.

fieldFixes.significance: The US Constitution never mentions privacy. Griswold inferred a right of privacy from the “penumbras” of the Bill of Rights, protecting an intimate relationship, marriage, and not just property or places. Later cases built a wider right to make personal decisions on this footing.
